rows: Samuel Morse, Daguerreotype by Draper

Dr. John William Draper, a chemist in New York, made some of the oldest surviving daguerreotype portraits in 1839 and 1840. This one is believed to show Samuel Morse, who invented the telegraph and Morse code.
Why would an inventor and a chemist be friends?
Draper Plate
This is one of a small group of very early daguerreotypes by Dr. John William Draper, a professor in New York. It is among the oldest surviving photographs of people in America.
Why would it be special to have a picture that old?
Theodore Frelinghuysen, Daguerreotype by Draper
John William Draper photographed a man believed to be Theodore Frelinghuysen, a New Jersey senator and college president, in 1839. It is one of the earliest American portraits.
What would it be like to sit still for minutes in the sun?
A Draper Portrait
This is another of Dr. Draper's earliest portraits from about 1840. Draper had to place his sitters on a rooftop in bright sun with their eyes closed or covered in powder to get a picture.
Why might sitters have to close their eyes?
Frieze on the Tower of the Winds, Athens

Joseph-Philibert Girault de Prangey photographed carvings on an ancient tower in Athens in 1842 with a daguerreotype camera. The Tower of the Winds is a 2,000-year-old clock tower with figures of the eight winds carved on its sides.
Can you find a figure that looks like it is blowing?
The Parthenon's North Colonnade
Girault de Prangey photographed the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens in 1842. His daguerreotypes are among the oldest pictures of the temple, showing it before restoration.
How many columns do you see?
Relief of Victory, Temple of Athena Nike
Girault de Prangey photographed a stone carving of the goddess Victory on the Acropolis in 1842. Photography let people study sculptures without traveling.
What is Victory doing in the carving?
Ancient Door, Magdalen College, Oxford
Talbot photographed an old oak door at Magdalen College in Oxford in the early 1840s. The calotype shows the weathered wood and carved stone, with soft shadows.
What does the grain of the wood look like?
Sir Robert Dennistoun's Tomb
Hill and Adamson photographed a tomb in Greyfriars Churchyard in Edinburgh. Hill and Adamson photographed in the graveyard because it had moody light and interesting monuments.
Why might a graveyard make a good place for photographs?
The Scott Monument Under Construction
Talbot photographed the Scott Monument in Edinburgh while scaffolding still surrounded it in 1844. It is a rare construction photograph from the early days of photography.
What can you see of how it was built?
A Mountain Rivulet at the Foot of Doune Castle
Talbot photographed a stream running below Doune Castle in Scotland in 1844. The water streaks across rocks in a soft calotype.
How does the water look in the picture?
Loch Katrine
Talbot photographed Loch Katrine in the Scottish Highlands in 1844 on his trip following the settings of Sir Walter Scott's poems. The still water and hills make the calotype glow.
Why would a poet's lake attract photographers?
Truman Smith
Truman Smith was a Whig congressman from Connecticut. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1840s as part of his series of famous Americans.
Why would a photographer want a gallery of politicians?
James Nasmyth, Inventor of the Steam Hammer
David Octavius Hill and Robert Adamson photographed James Nasmyth, who invented the steam hammer for forging iron. He was an engineer who also loved astronomy and made detailed drawings of the Moon.
What would an inventor of a giant hammer look like?
Cardinal Nicholas Wiseman
Nicholas Wiseman was the first Catholic Archbishop of Westminster, in England. Brady photographed him in the 1840s while he visited America.
What do you notice about his robe?
William Allen
William Allen was a Democratic senator from Ohio, nicknamed Earthquake Allen for his big voice. Brady photographed him in the 1840s.
Why might a politician have a nickname like Earthquake?
A Scene in York
Talbot photographed a street scene in the English city of York in 1845. The calotype shows medieval buildings, and few people moved enough to appear.
Why are the streets so empty?
Calvert Jones in the Sacristy of Lacock Abbey
Talbot photographed his friend Calvert Jones sitting in a church room at Lacock Abbey in 1845. Jones was a clergyman and an early photographer himself.
How does the stone room feel?
The Woodcutters
Talbot photographed woodcutters standing with an axe and a pile of logs in 1845. Staged working scenes like this showed that photography was good for everyday life.
What tools do the woodcutters have?
Hungerford Bridge
This calotype from 1845 shows Hungerford Bridge across the River Thames in London, designed by the engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel. It is one of the oldest photographs of London.
How is a suspension bridge different from other bridges?
Elizabeth Eastlake
Hill and Adamson photographed Elizabeth Rigby, who later became Lady Eastlake, an art writer. Their calotype portraits were praised for their soft light and strong mood.
What mood does the soft light give?
Branch of a Fern
Talbot photographed a fern branch in 1848. Plants were a favorite subject for him because he began his experiments with leaves and flowers.
How many parts does a fern leaf have?
Thomas Pratt
Thomas Pratt was a lawyer and politician from Maryland who served as governor and U.S. senator. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1840s or 1850s.
What would you ask a governor?
Frederick Langenheim
Frederick Langenheim and his brother William ran a studio in Philadelphia. They made some of the first photographs on glass slides, and Frederick was photographed around 1849.
How are photographs on glass different from paper?
Frederick Langenheim Looking at Talbotypes
Frederick Langenheim looks over some Talbotypes, the early paper photographs invented by Talbot. The Langenheims bought the American rights to Talbot's process in 1849.
Why would Frederick buy a process?
Pillar at Karnak
Maxime Du Camp photographed a tall pillar in the temple area at Karnak, Egypt, around 1850. He was traveling with the writer Gustave Flaubert.
Why would a writer travel with a photographer?
Franz Hanfstaengl
Alois Löcherer photographed Franz Hanfstaengl, a famous artist and lithographer in Munich, around 1850. Hanfstaengl later became one of the best photographers in Germany.
How can an artist become a photographer?
Barefoot Boy with a Hat and a Drumstick
A barefoot boy leans on a chair with a drumstick in a daguerreotype made around 1850. Children were photographed with toys to keep them still.
What kind of toys can you hold while sitting still?
Justus von Liebig
Justus von Liebig was a German chemist who helped to create modern chemistry and invented fertilizer. Alois Löcherer photographed him around 1850.
What would a chemist look like?
Maidu Boy
Robert H. Vance made this ambrotype, a photograph on glass, of a boy from the Maidu people of California around 1850. Vance had a gallery in San Francisco in the Gold Rush years.
What do you think the boy thinks about being photographed?
The Bridge of Palalda
Gustave Le Gray photographed the old bridge of Palalda near Amélie-les-Bains in France in 1851. The government sent him and a colleague on a trip to record old monuments.
How is an arched stone bridge built?
The Salon of 1852
Gustave Le Gray photographed the art exhibition called the Salon of 1852 at the Palais-Royal in Paris. Paintings hung from floor to ceiling.
How would you hang so many paintings?
Louis Figuier
Nadar photographed Louis Figuier, a French scientist and writer of popular science books. Nadar's friends were often writers, artists and scientists.
What would a science writer be doing?
Saint-Honorat, near Arles
Édouard Baldus photographed the old Roman cemetery of Saint-Honorat near Arles, France, in 1853, on a trip to Provence. The long avenue of stone tombs gave a ruined, ancient mood.
What makes a graveyard look ancient?
Pierre-Jean David d'Angers
Édouard Baldus photographed a statue of the sculptor David d'Angers. David d'Angers was a famous French sculptor who made many monuments.
Why might a sculptor like to be photographed?
Head of the Harbour, Balaklava
Roger Fenton photographed the head of the harbor at Balaklava during the Crimean War, crowded with ships bringing supplies. Looking at it you can see how important the harbor was.
How many ships can you count?
Plateau of Sebastopol
Fenton photographed the plateau above Sevastopol, where armies camped for a long siege. The empty, rocky ground is dotted with tents.
What would living on a plateau in winter be like?
The Town of Balaklava
Fenton photographed the small port town of Balaklava from the heights. In 1855 it became a huge base for the British army.
What do you notice about the shape of the harbor?
Artillery Wagons, Balaklava in the Distance
Fenton photographed wagons for the artillery with the harbor of Balaklava far behind. His war pictures show the logistics behind the fighting.
What do the wagons carry?
Archibald Gordon
Archibald Gordon was the chief medical officer for part of the British army in the Crimea. Fenton photographed doctors and officers.
What would a doctor do in a war?
Group of Croat Chiefs
Fenton photographed a group of Croatian soldiers who fought for the Ottoman army in the Crimean War. Their colorful uniforms stand out in the camp.
What details of their clothes can you see?
Omar Pasha
Omar Pasha was the Ottoman general who fought the Russians in the Crimean War. Fenton photographed him in 1855 in the Crimea.
What does a general's face show?
Harbour, Swansea, Wales
Alfred Rosling, a timber merchant and amateur photographer, photographed the harbor of Swansea in Wales. Fishing boats and cargo ships rest near the shore.
What kinds of boats do you see?
Battery, Malakoff
Léon-Eugène Méhédin photographed the Malakoff battery, a fort the French captured at Sevastopol in 1855. He worked as an official war photographer for the French army.
Why is the fort so important?
Mother and Child
A mother holds her child in this portrait from the mid-1850s. The photographer used the sunlight and soft pose to make the picture look like a painted Madonna.
How does a mother hold a child so tenderly?
Inclined Plane F, Delaware and Hudson Canal
Thomas H. Johnson made large photographs of the Delaware and Hudson Canal in the 1850s. Boats were pulled up a sloping track called an inclined plane.
How would you move a boat uphill?
Temple Tank, Tamil Nadu
An unknown photographer showed a Hindu temple with its large water tank in Tamil Nadu in southern India. Tanks like these are used for ritual bathing.
Why would a temple have a big pool?
The Return of the Fleet
Gustave Le Gray photographed ships returning to the French coast. He is famous for dramatic seascapes where sky and sea are both sharp.
How do you think he made sky and sea both look right?
Hollow Oak Tree, Fontainebleau
Gustave Le Gray photographed an old hollow oak in the forest of Fontainebleau. Painters and photographers loved the forest's ancient trees.
How old do you think the tree is?
Study of the Sky
Charles Marville photographed clouds in the sky. It is a very early picture of a cloudy sky, which was hard to catch.
What kind of weather do you think it was?
The Taj Mahal
The Getty Museum owns this photograph of the Taj Mahal from about 1855 to 1865 by Francis Frith. The great white marble tomb in Agra, India, was built by Shah Jahan for his wife.
Why would an emperor build such a big tomb?
Edward Bates
Edward Bates was a lawyer from Missouri who became Abraham Lincoln's attorney general. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1850s.
What does an attorney general do?
Andrew Johnson
Andrew Johnson, a tailor from Tennessee, became the 17th president of the United States after Lincoln's death. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1850s.
What would you look at in a future president's face?
Sandy Path Uphill, Fontainebleau
Gustave Le Gray photographed a sandy road climbing through the forest of Fontainebleau. The glowing path and dark trees make it look like a painting.
Where do you think the path leads?
The Cathedral from Corso Francesco, Milan
Léon Gérard, an amateur from Paris, photographed the huge cathedral of Milan, Italy, in 1857. The white marble spires fill the picture.
How many spires can you count?
